meta.title: Quilted Languages
meta.tagline: How empires shaped the words of Romania and Japan

romania.summary: Family words are the oldest layer. Frate descends directly from the Latin that formed the base of Romanian.
romania.blogTitle: Romanian in pre-history — the Latin foundation
blog: Frate — the word frate, meaning brother, is a very clear direct descendent of the word fratus in Latin, the language which formed the base of the Romanian language. Just like in most other languages, words describing familial relations often were retained by their descendents.

japan.summary: From oto + hito, "young person". Family words survived from the mother tongue across millennia.
japan.blogTitle: Japanese in pre-history — native family words
blog: 弟 — the word for little brother, "otouto", derives from a combination of two older Japanese words, oto and hito, meaning a young person. This word shifted in pronunciation and meaning over millennia, but is a poster child of the phenomenon of familial relation words being retained from mother tongues.

romania.summary: South Slavs reached southeastern Europe in the 6th century. Old Church Slavonic became the liturgical language of Moldavia and Wallachia.
romania.blogTitle: Romanian in the year 500 — Slavic migrations
blog: Iubire — this Romanian word for love has origins in the South Slavic languages, from which Romanian borrowed extensively over the course of centuries of cross-cultural communication and experience. The South Slavs first migrated to southeastern Europe around the 6th century, and from there spread throughout the Balkan mountain range, bringing with them their unique language.
Old Church Slavonic specifically served as the liturgical language in the principalities of Moldavia and Wallachia for many years and marked Romanian permanently with its influence.

japan.summary: Middle Chinese 'love' arrived through Buddhist texts in the 6th century, where it meant attachment and desire.
japan.blogTitle: Japanese in the year 500 — Buddhism arrives
blog: 愛 (ai) — the word for love most commonly used today in Japan has its origins in medieval China, where the Middle Chinese word for love first made its leap onto the Japanese archipelago through the extensive literature of the Chinese intelligentsia and religions, especially Buddhism.
Buddhism made its splash in Japan in the 6th century when it was endorsed by Prince Shōtoku Taishi. Its original usage in Buddhist texts describing attachment and desire has shifted over time.

Other early Buddhist borrowings include 人間 (ningen), human being — interestingly, the readings "nin" and "gen" are no longer used for these characters outside of this context — as well as 愛情 (aijō), love, and 友情 (yūjō), friendship.

romania.summary: Much of Romanian cuisine was cemented under Ottoman and Greek rule, and the food words came with it.
romania.blogTitle: Romanian in the 1400s — the Ottoman kitchen
blog: Chiftea — meatball. This word was borrowed from Ottoman Turkish, which itself borrowed the word from Persian. It's a pretty easy example to understand — much of modern Romanian cuisine was formed and cemented under Ottoman and Greek rule.

Ciorbă, musaca, pilaf: all common foods in Romania today continue to use the words that the Ottomans first brought to the principalities of Wallachia and Moldova. Food words are common borrowings, and often reflect the culinary neighborhoods of their countries of origin.

japan.summary: Successive waves of Chinese influence arrived through trade and scholarship. Each era's pronunciation survives as a distinct 'reading' of the same characters.
japan.blogTitle: Japanese in the 1400s — later waves from China
blog: Japan received successive waves of Chinese influence through trade and scholarship, each era's pronunciation preserved as distinct 'readings' of the same characters. [Draft — section not yet written.]

romania.summary: Transylvania's Romanians lived for centuries inside the Hungarian Kingdom, adding words from yet another non-Romance language.
romania.blogTitle: Romanian in the 1600s — at the crossroads of empires
blog: Romanians lived, for hundreds of years, at the crossroads of multiple empires. While Ottoman, Slavic, and Byzantine influence dominated the southern and eastern principalities of Wallachia and Moldova, the Transylvanian principality, which also had many Romanians, existed as part of a vast Hungarian Kingdom for many years, introducing many words from yet another non-Romance language into Romanian.

The word for city, oraș, comes from the Hungarian város, which itself comes from vár, the Hungarian word for castle. Political, historical and linguistic relationships helped to form the diversity of the Romanian language today.

japan.summary: Through a few tightly controlled ports, Portuguese and Dutch traders left words in science, industry and imported goods.
japan.blogTitle: Japanese in the 1600s — Portuguese and Dutch traders
blog: By the 1600s, Japan had started opening up to the world, albeit very slowly, and only to very specific groups, and only in very specific ports. So maybe they weren't really opening up. Nevertheless, the Portuguese and Dutch made a mark on Japanese through their early loanwords in the fields of science, industry, and western imports to the medieval Tokugawa shogunate.
かるた (karuta) was once the Portuguese word for cards (cartas) and now refers to one specific card game in Japan, after centuries of shifting meanings.
ビー玉 (bīdama), marble, is half Portuguese (vidro, glass) and half Japanese 玉 (tama, ball) — a word that shows the way linguistic barriers are really only half as real as we make them out to be.

romania.summary: 'Re-Latinization': Slavonic words were purged in favour of French ones, and the alphabet switched from Cyrillic to Latin.
blog: The age of nationalism. Romania underwent 're-Latinization' — purging Slavonic words and adopting French vocabulary, switching from Cyrillic to a modified Latin alphabet. [Draft — section not yet written.]

japan.summary: The Meiji Restoration blended English parliamentarianism with Prussian monarchy and imported words from both.
japan.blogTitle: Japanese in the 1850s — the Meiji opening
blog: The age of nationalism. Japan's Meiji Restoration blended English parliamentarianism and Prussian monarchy, importing words from both. [Draft — section not yet written.]

romania.summary: Soviet domination brought Russian political vocabulary into everyday Romanian speech.
romania.blogTitle: Romanian in the 1950s — behind the Iron Curtain
blog: After WWII, Soviet domination brought Russian into Romanian — tovarăș (comrade) entered everyday speech alongside communist ideology. [Draft — section not yet written.]

japan.summary: The American occupation brought a flood of English loanwords.
japan.blogTitle: Japanese in the 1950s — the American occupation
blog: After WWII, the American occupation flooded Japanese with English loanwords. [Draft — section not yet written.]
